source_text: Proprium iam negotium passus meae opinionis Latine quoque ostendam virgines nostras velari oportere ex quo transitum aetatis suae fecerint: hoc exigere veritatem, cui nemo praescribere potest, non spatium temporum, non patrocinia personarum, non privilegium regionum. Ex his enim fere consuetudo initium ab aliqua ignorantia vel simplicitate sortita in usum per successionem corroboratur et ita adversus veritatem vindicatur. Sed dominus noster Christus veritatem se, non consuetudinem, cognominavit. Si semper Christus, et prior omnibus, aeque veritas sempiterna et antiqua res. Viderint ergo quibus novum est quod sibi vetus est. Haereses non tam novitas quam veritas revincit. Quodcumque adversus veritatem sapit, hoc erit haeresis, etiam vetus consuetudo. Ceterum suo vitio quis quid ignorat. Quod autem ignoratur fuit tam requirendum quam recipiendum quod agnoscitur. Regula quidem fidei una omnino est, sola immobilis et irreformabilis, credendi scilicet in unicum deum omnipotentem, mundi conditorem, et filium eius Iesum Christum, natum ex virgine Maria, crucifixum sub Pontio Pilato, tertia die resuscitatum a mortuis, receptum in caelis, sedentem nunc ad dexteram patris, venturum iudicare vivos et mortuos per carnis etiam resurrectionem. Hac lege fidei manente cetera iam disciplinae et conversationis admittunt novitatem correctionis, operante scilicet et proficiente usque in finem gratia dei. Quale est enim, ut diabolo semper operante et adiciente cottidie ad iniquitatis ingenia opus dei aut cessaverit aut proficere destiterit? cum propterea paracletum miserit dominus, ut, quoniam humana mediocritas omnia semel capere non poterat, paulatim dirigeretur et ordinaretur et ad perfectum perduceretur disciplina ab illo vicario domini, spiritu sancto. Adhuc, inquit, multa habeo loqui vobis, sed nondum potestis ea baiulare: cum venerit ille spiritus veritatis, deducet vos in omnem veritatem et supervenientia renuntiabit vobis. Sed et supra de hoc eius opere pronuntiavit. Quae est ergo paracleti administratio, nisi haec, quod disciplina dirigitur, quod scripturae revelantur, quod intellectus reformatur, quod ad meliora proficitur? Nihil sine acta(??)e est, omnia tempus expectant. Denique Ecclesiastes, Tempas, inquit, omni rei. Aspice ipsam creaturam paulatim ad fru(??) promoveri. Granum est primo, et de grano frutex oritur, et de frutice arbuscula enititur. deinde rami et frondes invalescunt et tetum arboris nomen expanditur, inde germinis tumor et flos de germine solvitur, et de flore fructus aperitur: is quoque rudis aliquamdiu et informis paulatim aetatem suam dirigens eruditur in mansuetudinem saporis. Sic et iustitia (nam idem deus i(??)slitiae et creaturae) primo fuit in rudimentis, natura deum metuens: dehinc per legem et prophetas promovit in infantiam, dehinc per evangelium efferbuit in iuventutem, nunc per paracletum componitur in maturitatem. Hic erit solus a Christo magister et dicendos et verendus. Non enim ab se loquitur, sed quae mandantur a Christo. Hic solus antecessor, quia solus post Christum. Hunc qui receperunt, veritatem consuetudini anteponunt. Hunc qui audierunt usque, non olim, prophetantem, virgines contegunt.
thought_title: Truth, not custom, must govern veiling
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by stating his thesis that virgins must be veiled once they reach maturity, and begins arguing that truth, not custom, must rule church discipline.
pass_a_gloss: Having now undertaken the proper business of my opinion, I will show also in Latin that our virgins ought to be veiled from the time when they have made the passage of their age. This truth demands, to which no one can prescribe, not the space of times, not the patronage of persons, not the privilege of regions. For from these things custom, having generally obtained its beginning from some ignorance or simplicity, is strengthened into use through succession, and thus is vindicated against truth. But our Lord Christ named himself truth, not custom. If Christ is always, and prior to all things, equally truth is an everlasting and ancient thing. Let them see to it, then, to whom what is old to them is new. Heresies are refuted not so much by novelty as by truth. Whatever savors against truth, this will be heresy, even old custom. For the rest, by his own fault each person is ignorant of something. But what is unknown was as much to be sought as what is recognized is to be received. The rule of faith indeed is one altogether, alone immovable and unreformable, namely of believing in one God almighty, maker of the world, and his son Jesus Christ, born from the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised from the dead on the third day, received in the heavens, sitting now at the right hand of the father, going to come to judge the living and the dead through the resurrection also of the flesh. While this law of faith remains, the other things of discipline and conduct admit the novelty of correction, as the grace of God works and advances even to the end. For what kind of thing is it, that while the devil always works and adds daily to the devices of iniquity, the work of God should either have ceased or stopped advancing? Since for this reason the Lord sent the Holy Spirit, so that, since human mediocrity could not grasp all things at once, discipline should be directed and ordered gradually and led to perfection by that vicar of the Lord, the Holy Spirit. He says, 'Still I have many things to say to you, but you cannot yet bear them: when that spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth and will announce to you the things that are coming.' But also above he declared concerning this work of his. What then is the administration of the Holy Spirit, except this, that discipline is directed, that the Scriptures are revealed, that the understanding is reformed, that progress is made toward better things? Nothing is without its season, all things await their time. Finally Ecclesiastes says, 'There is a time for every thing.' Look at creation itself being promoted gradually to fruit. First it is a grain, and from the grain a shoot arises, and from the shoot a little tree struggles forth. Then branches and leaves grow strong and the whole name of a tree is spread out, then the swelling of a bud, and a flower is released from the bud, and from the flower the fruit is opened: this too, for a while rough and unformed, gradually directing its own age, is trained into the mildness of flavor. So also righteousness (for the same God is of righteousness and of creation) was first in its rudiments, nature fearing God: then through the law and the prophets it advanced into infancy, then through the gospel it boiled up into youth, now through the Holy Spirit it is composed into maturity. He alone will be the teacher to be named and to be revered after Christ. For he does not speak from himself, but what things are commanded by Christ. He alone is the forerunner, because he alone is after Christ. Those who have received him put truth before custom. Those who have heard him prophesying even until now, not long ago, cover their virgins.

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of 'transitum' as a crossing or passage, matching Tertullian's metaphor of moving from girlhood to womanhood.

bible_refs.note: Adhuc multa habeo loqui vobis, sed nondum potestis ea baiulare: cum venerit ille spiritus veritatis, deducet vos in omnem veritatem et supervenientia renuntiabit vobis.

pass_b_english: I have now taken up the cause of my own view, and I will show in Latin as well that our virgins ought to be veiled from the moment they have passed into womanhood. Truth demands this, and no one can set limits to truth: not the passage of time, not the patronage of important persons, not the privilege of any region. For it is from these things that custom generally takes its beginning. Born from some ignorance or simplicity, custom is strengthened into use by succession, and in this way it asserts its claim against truth.

But our Lord Christ named himself truth, not custom. If Christ is always, and prior to all things, then truth is equally everlasting and ancient. Let those to whom what is old seems new look to it. It is not so much novelty as truth that refutes heresies. Whatever savors against truth will be heresy, even if it is an old custom. Besides, if anyone is ignorant of something, that is his own fault. What is unknown ought to be sought out just as much as what is known ought to be received.

The rule of faith is indeed altogether one, alone immovable and unreformable: namely, to believe in one God almighty, maker of the world, and in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised from the dead on the third day, received into heaven, now seated at the right hand of the Father, coming to judge the living and the dead through the resurrection of the flesh as well. While this law of faith remains, everything else of discipline and conduct admits the novelty of correction, as the grace of God works and advances even to the end.

For what kind of thing is it that, while the devil is always working and adding daily to the devices of wickedness, the work of God should either have ceased or stopped advancing? The Lord sent the Holy Spirit for this very reason: because human limitation could not grasp everything at once, discipline should be gradually directed, ordered, and brought to perfection by the Holy Spirit, who acts in the Lord's place. He says, "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; when that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth and will announce to you the things that are coming" (John 16:12-13). But he also declared this work of his above.

What then is the administration of the Holy Spirit except this: that discipline is directed, that Scriptures are revealed, that understanding is reformed, that progress is made toward better things? Nothing is without its act; all things await their time. Finally Ecclesiastes says, "There is a time for every matter" (Ecclesiastes 3:1). Look at creation itself: it is advanced gradually toward fruit. First there is a grain, and from the grain a shoot arises, and from the shoot a little tree struggles forth. Then branches and leaves grow strong, and the whole name of tree is spread out; then the swelling of the bud comes, and the flower is released from the bud, and from the flower the fruit is opened. This too, for some time rough and unformed, gradually directing its own age, is trained into the gentleness of flavor.

So also righteousness, for the same God is God of righteousness and of creation, was at first in its rudiments, fearing God by nature; then through the law and the prophets it advanced into infancy; then through the gospel it boiled over into youth; now through the Holy Spirit it is composed into maturity. He alone will be the teacher from Christ, to be named and revered. For he does not speak from himself, but what is commanded by Christ. He alone is the forerunner, because he alone comes after Christ. Those who have received him set truth before custom. Those who have heard him prophesying until now, not long ago, cover their virgins.
notes: OCR damage: 'acta(??)e' likely 'aetate' (season/age); 'fru(??)' likely 'fructum' (fruit); 'i(??)slitiae' likely 'iustitiae' (of righteousness). Gloss reflects these readings.

polish.changed: Clarified the Holy Spirit's role as acting in the Lord's place, smoothed sentence order, and made the progression of thought easier to follow aloud.

notes.quote: that vicar of the Lord, the Holy Spirit
notes.why: 'Vicar of the Lord' is a technical title; reader may not know what 'vicar' means here.

last_rejected.quote: the swelling of the bud comes, and the flower is released from the bud
last_rejected.source_quote: germinis tumor et flos de germine solvitur
last_rejected.why: tumor is swelling; flos is the subject of solvitur. English splits one clause and makes 'swelling comes' a separate clause.
last_rejected.fix: then the swelling of the bud, and the flower is released from the bud
last_rejected.ruling: Latin says “tumor … et flos … solvitur”; translation adds “comes” for swelling, a stylistic paraphrase, not a change of core meaning.

problems.quote: He alone is to be called and revered as teacher after Christ.
problems.source_quote: Hic erit solus a Christo magister et dicendos et verendus.
problems.why: a Christo means the teacher comes from Christ, not after him; erit is future. 'After' belongs to the next sentence.
problems.fix: He alone will be the teacher from Christ, to be both named and revered.
problems.ruling: 'a Christo magister' means teacher from Christ, not 'after'; 'erit' is future ('will be'); 'solus post Christum' appears in the next sentence. English misstates the relation.

edits.old: He alone is to be called and revered as teacher after Christ.
edits.new: He alone will be the teacher from Christ, to be named and revered.

fixed: Fixed mistranslation: 'a Christo' means 'from Christ' (source) not 'after Christ', and 'erit' is future 'will be'; 'after Christ' belongs to the next sentence's 'post Christum'.

last_rejected.why: The damaged word is aetate (age/season), matching the time theme; “act” is not the sense.
last_rejected.fix: Nothing is without its age; all things await their time.
last_rejected.ruling: Source reads "acta(??)e", damaged; "act" is a literal reading of acta, but the sense is uncertain and minor; the following "omnia tempus expectant" makes it ambiguous. Not a clear major error.

last_rejected.quote: prophesying until now, not long ago
last_rejected.why: non olim contrasts with usque: not merely formerly. English “not long ago” means recently.
last_rejected.fix: Those who have heard him prophesying up to the present, not of old, cover their virgins.
last_rejected.ruling: "usque, non olim" means "until now, not long ago"; non olim = recently, so "not long ago" is within normal range.
